newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's pastoral land open to Aboriginal claims.
newsitem.headline: Australia's pastoral land open to Aboriginal claims.

text.p: Australia's High Court on Monday threw open the nation's farms to Aboriginal claims when it ruled that land given to farmers by government grant could still be claimed by Aborigines under "native title" laws.
The landmark ruling prompted Australian farmers to warn of a rash of new native title claims within weeks, leaving the farming industry in state of uncertainty.
"I suspect that pretty well every pastoral lease (land grant) in Australia will be under claim within a few weeks," said National Farmers' Federation president Donald McGauchie.
"We are looking at 20 years of protracted litigation to determine where native title continues to exist and in what form," McGauchie told reporters.
The chief minister of the outback Northern Territory said 96 percent of the 1.34 million sq kms (520,000 sq miles) of territory was now vulnerable to Aboriginal native title.
Shane Stone said the High Court ruling left "a confused and chaotic regime that will see native title applications determined on almost all pastoral leases".
But Aborigines rejected such claims as scaremongering.
Lawyer James Fitzgerald, who represented Aborigines in the High Court, said the decision was a win for both farmers and Aborigines.
"The High Court has made it clear that wherever the rights of pastoralists are in conflict with the exercise of native title rights that the rights of pastoralists will prevail," Fitzgerald said.
"As a result, there is no loser from today's decision."
Australia's highest court on Monday upheld a native title claim by the Aboriginal Wik people to more than 35,000 sq kms (13,500 sq miles) of land in far-north Queensland state.
It ruled that the Wik people's right to certain areas of land would co-exist with those of the pastoral leaseholders. If those rights conflicted, however, the leaseholder will have precedence.

The Wik were appealing an earlier ruling in Australia's Federal Court that found 12 pastoral leases extinguished Aboriginal land claims. The Wik will now go back to the Federal Court to prove their right to the land.

In 1992, the High Court overturned the historical idea of Terra Nullius -- that Australia was an empty land when white settlers arrived in 1788 -- thus recognising that Aborigines had traditional land rights.
In 1993, the Australian government passed native title laws allowing Aborigines to claim land if they could prove uninterrupted traditional usage of the land.
But there has been much confusion as to exactly where native title applies.

In most areas where pastoral leases occur Aborigines were forced off the land, but in the outback some Aborigines still live a traditional life over vast tracts of resource-rich land which has been under pastoral lease.
Many in the resource sector fear the High Court's ruling will mean mining firms will be denied access to this resource-rich land.
There are more than 450 native title claims pending.
National Native Title Tribunal Judge Robert French said each claim over pastoral leases would have to be judged on a case-by-case basis.
The NFF's McGauchie called on the Australian government to introduce legislation to protect the rights of farmers, whose activity is crucial to the Australian economy.
The gross value of Australian farm production is forecast at A$25.8 billion (US$20 billion) in the year to June 30, 1997

"I think we have to deal with the fact that this is going to create massive uncertainty -- a great many industries are going to grind to halt over this and there's going to be an enormous cost in litigation," McGauchie said.
